stops.name: Venice, first grade: the seven pillars and the planets
stops.campa: On the lowest and most honored grade of the Theatre, Camillo places not the seven Sephirot themselves, too remote from ordinary understanding, but the seven planets that stand in for them: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, each ranked with its Sephirah and its governing angel. Ancient theatres seated the great in the lowest rows; Camillo does the same with meaning, since from these fundamental measures, once truly known, the mind can climb into the supercelestial world of the Ideas or descend into the elemental world spread out above.
stops.quote: Solomon in the ninth chapter of Proverbs says that wisdom has built herself a house and has founded it on seven pillars. By these columns, signifying most stable eternity, we are to understand the seven Sephiroth of the supercelestial world, which are the seven measures of the fabric of the celestial and inferior worlds.
stops.quote_source: L'Idea del Theatro, p. 9, trans. Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Venice, the Banquet, second grade
stops.campa: Above the planets, Camillo sets the image of a Banquet on every gate of the second grade: Homer's tale that Ocean once feasted all the gods together. Ocean, Camillo explains, is the waters of wisdom that existed before all created matter, and the feasting gods are the divine Ideas gathering to bring forth the world. It is his image for the first day of creation, the elements still simple and unmixed, and he means the reader, gazing at banquet after banquet across seven gates, to feel Genesis itself, In the beginning, opening beneath the picture.
stops.quote: The second grade of the Theatre will have depicted on all its gates the same image, and this will be a banquet. Homer feigns that Ocean made a banquet for all the gods, nor was it without lofty mysterious meanings that this lofty poet invented this fiction.
stops.quote_source: L'Idea del Theatro, p. 17, trans. Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Venice, the Cave of the Nymphs, third grade
stops.campa: The third grade rises with a Cave on every gate: not Plato's cave of shadows, Camillo is careful to say, but the Cave of the Nymphs from Homer's Odyssey, where nymphs weave at looms of stone and bees pass ceaselessly in and out. Following Porphyry's ancient reading of that cave, Camillo makes the weaving nymphs and laboring bees stand for the mixing of the four simple elements into all the compounded things of the world, each cave keeping, planet by planet, the particular mixture proper to its nature.
stops.quote: The third grade will have depicted on each of its gates a Cave, which we call the Homeric Cave to differentiate it from that which Plato describes in his Republic.
stops.quote_source: L'Idea del Theatro, p. 29, trans. Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Venice, the Gorgon Sisters, fourth grade
stops.campa: The fourth grade belongs to the interior man, mind and soul, the noblest of God's creatures made in his own image. Its image, strange to a first glance, is Hesiod's three Gorgon Sisters, who share only a single eye between them. Camillo takes this from Kabbalist teaching on the three souls of man, vegetable, sensitive, and rational, seeing through one another as the sisters see through their one eye. Behind each gate wait the volumes proper to the interior man, ranked planet by planet, so that the whole science of the soul stands open at this level of the climb.
stops.quote: Let us now rise to the fourth grade belonging to the interior man, the most noble of God's creatures, which He made in his own image and similitude.
stops.quote_source: L'Idea del Theatro, p. 53, trans. Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Venice, Pasiphae and the Bull, fifth grade
stops.campa: On the fifth grade the soul is joined at last to the body, and the leading image is Pasiphae enamoured of the Bull: for the Platonists teach that the descending soul, changing its fiery vehicle for an airy one as it falls through the spheres, comes at last to desire gross matter itself, exactly as the queen of Crete desired the beast. Beneath this image on every gate wait the sciences of the exterior man, his body's parts and humors, each assigned, at the foot of the gate, to its ruling sign of the zodiac.
stops.quote: For she, being enamoured of the Bull, signifies the soul which, according to the Platonists, falls into a state of desiring the body.
stops.quote_source: L'Idea del Theatro, p. 67, trans. Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Venice, the Sandals of Mercury, sixth grade
stops.campa: The sixth grade is crowned on every gate with the winged Sandals of Mercury, which the poets say the messenger god puts on when he goes to execute the will of the gods. Under this image Camillo files everything a man can do by nature alone, without the aid of any learned art: the plain activities of ordinary human life, walking, working, trading, ruling a household. It is the grade just below the arts proper, the last rung before invention, the ordinary motion of the world before Prometheus brings down his fire.
stops.quote: The sixth grade of the Theatre has on each of the gates of the planets the Sandals, and other ornaments, which Mercury puts on when he goes to execute the will of the gods, as the poets feign. Thereby the memory will be awakened to find beneath them all the operations which man can perform naturally, and without any art.
stops.quote_source: L'Idea del Theatro, trans. Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Venice, Prometheus, seventh grade
stops.campa: At the summit, the seventh and highest grade, Camillo sets Prometheus with his stolen, lighted torch above every gate: the Titan who taught men the arts and sciences of the gods. Under this image he files all the noble arts and the vile ones alike, and religion, and law, the full harvest of human invention built on everything the lower six grades have laid down. The design is complete in idea, though not one board of it is yet cut: from the simple elements of the Banquet to the fire of Prometheus, the entire chain of being, ranked and locatable at a glance.
stops.quote: The seventh grade is assigned to all the arts, both noble and vile, and above each gate is Prometheus with a lighted torch.
stops.quote_source: L'Idea del Theatro, trans. Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Venice, departure for France with Rangone and Muzio
stops.campa: Word of the design, and perhaps of a beginning of the carpentry, reaches the French ambassador in Venice, Lazare de Baïf, who carries report of it to his king. In 1530 Camillo sets out for France in the company of Count Claudio Rangone and his loyal friend Girolamo Muzio, a courtier who will stand at Camillo's side, on and off, for the rest of his life and will be the one, fourteen years hence, to take down his dying words. Camillo leaves Italy still a schoolmaster of local fame; he means to return the confidant of a king.

stops.name: Fontainebleau, before Francis I
stops.campa: Camillo is brought before Francis I, patron already of Leonardo's old age and soon to be the builder of a whole gallery of allegory at Fontainebleau. He lays out the Idea of a theatre that will hold, ranked and legible, the sum of everything Cicero and the ancients ever knew, and hints at deeper secrets besides, Kabbalist and Hermetic, to be given to no other man alive but the king. Francis is captivated. He gives Camillo money toward the work, with the promise of more, on the single condition that Camillo publish nothing of it without his royal leave.

stops.name: Venice, the return to perfect the work
stops.campa: Camillo returns to Italy to bring the wooden Theatre nearer completion before showing it again at the French court, and in Venice he sets down, in a manuscript discourse on his own project, the philosophical ground beneath the carpentry: a borrowed idea from Avicenna, that the human soul carries within it a hidden power to act upon the outer world, to bend things to its will, wherever the soul's affection for a thing is great enough. It is the same claim, restated in the language of the philosophers, that the Theatre itself will make silently through its images: that to see rightly is already to hold power.
stops.quote: Avicenna's conclusions in the sixth book on nature are very appealing to me, where he says that there is a certain capacity in our soul to change things and to make them obey us, while our soul is attracted by a great affection for them.
stops.quote_source: Discorso in materia del suo theatro (1532), trans. in Bolzoni, The Gallery of Memory

stops.name: Padua, Viglius Zuichemus hears the rumor
stops.campa: In Padua the young Frisian jurist Viglius Zuichemus, a correspondent and admirer of Erasmus, hears everyone talking of a certain Giulio Camillo who has built, they say, a wonderful amphitheatre: whoever is admitted to it as spectator will be able to discourse on any subject as fluently as Cicero himself. Viglius takes it at first for a traveler's fable, until Battista Egnazio, a scholar he trusts, confirms that the thing is real: an architect who has drawn up, in certain fixed places, everything that can be found in Cicero, arranged by orders and grades with stupendous labor and, Viglius begins to suspect, something more than merely human skill.

stops.name: Venice, Viglius inspects the wooden Theatre
stops.campa: Viglius travels to Venice and Camillo himself admits him: an object big enough for two men to stand inside together, of wood, marked with many images, and full of little boxes, various orders and grades rising around them. Camillo shows him mass upon mass of paper, sentences of Cicero broken down and refiled by subject until Viglius, who thought he knew how rich an author Cicero was, is astonished at how much more can be drawn out of him. Camillo stammers over Latin, his pen having half-ruined his spoken tongue, but grows fluent and strange the moment he begins to explain, as though stupefied himself, what the Theatre means and does.
stops.quote: A built or constructed mind and soul... a windowed one. All things that the human mind can conceive, and which we cannot see with the corporeal eye, after being collected together by diligent meditation, may be expressed by certain corporeal signs in such a way that the beholder may at once perceive with his eyes everything that is otherwise hidden in the depths of the human mind.
stops.quote_source: Camillo's own description of the Theatre, recorded in Viglius Zuichemus's letter to Erasmus, 8 June 1532 (Erasmus, Epistolae, ed. Allen, X, pp. 29-30)
